title: Finding who decides: the tracing method

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
Tracing who decides is a fixed sequence of six steps that takes a proposal to the body that can turn it into policy, and to the power that body would use.

  1. Name the instrument the proposal needs: an Act; a rule or regulation under an existing Act; a rate, order or other notification under an existing Act. Or say none is needed: an executive decision, such as a scheme, can act without a new law.
  2. Find whose subject it is: the Union, the States or both. The answer comes from the Seventh Schedule under Article 246 of the Constitution, or from a provision of an Act that already covers the matter.
  3. Find the body that holds the power to make that instrument, and the numbered provision that gives it the power. For a scheme, that provision is the executive power of the Union (Article 73) or of the State (Article 162), used by the decision that approved it, such as a Cabinet approval.
  4. Find the process the instrument must pass before it binds, such as previous publication of a draft for objections, an approval, notification in the Gazette, commencement on a notified date, and laying before the legislature. Not every instrument passes all of these, and they are not always in this order: a regulation, for example, is laid before Parliament after it is made and notified.
  5. List every other body whose agreement the process requires, and the bodies or officers who carry the decision out.
  6. State the result in one sentence: X decides, under Y, by process Z, with W’s agreement.

blocks.label: In plain terms
blocks.html:
Step 1. Name the instrument. What would have to exist on paper for the proposal to be policy? If you cannot name one, the proposal is not yet ready to trace.

Step 2. Find whose subject it is. If an Act already covers the matter, read what it says about itself. If not, find the entry in the Seventh Schedule’s three lists.

Step 3. Find the body and the provision. Which body can make that instrument? Which numbered section or article gives it the power? “The government” is not a body. “The minister” is usually not the holder of the power.

Step 4. Find the process. What must happen before the instrument binds anyone?

Step 5. List who else must agree, and who carries it out. A body whose approval the process needs is a second decider.

Step 6. Write one sentence. X decides, under Y, by process Z, with W’s agreement.

The trace can stop, because the documents you have do not answer a step. Then write down where it stopped, the candidates, and the document that would settle it.

Or the trace can find that the decision was taken years ago. Then your proposal is really about carrying the decision out, and it goes to different people.

A finished trace tells you who can act. It never tells you whether they will.

blocks.label: Illustration 1
blocks.html:
Start with a trace that does not finish. Your department’s made-up proposal reads: “The Health Department should ban junk food in school canteens in the district.”

Step 1. The instrument. “Ban” could mean a regulation, an order from the State to its own schools, or a new Act. The proposal does not say which. “Junk food” has no definition, so no instrument could be written from it. Before you trace, rewrite the proposal so that a body could act on it: “School canteens in the district should not sell sugar-sweetened drinks.”

Step 2. Whose subject. Look first for an Act that already covers food sold in canteens. The Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 (the FSS Act) does. It defines a food business as any undertaking, “whether public or private”, that handles food, and the definition “includes food services, catering services, sale of food”. Its definition of premises names “food canteens”. Section 2 declares that “the Union should take under its control the food industry”. Now put that beside entry 52 of the Union List: “Industries, the control of which by the Union is declared by Parliament by law to be expedient in the public interest.” The words match. The Act does not name the entry. The match is your reading, and you should say so in a note.

But a school canteen is also part of a school. Education is entry 25 of the Concurrent List, and public health is entry 6 of the State List. So a second route is open: the State acting for the schools it runs. The section on where a body’s power comes from showed that a State’s executive power reaches as far as its Legislature’s power to make laws (Article 162).

Step 3. Body and provision. Route one is the Food Authority, which makes regulations under section 92(1) of the FSS Act “with the previous approval of the Central Government and after previous publication”. Route two is the State Government, through its school education department, under its executive power.

Here the trace forks, and the documents in hand cannot close the fork. They do not say whether the Food Authority has already made a regulation on what school canteens may sell. They do not say whether Chhattisgarh has issued an order. They do not say how far the Food Authority’s duty under section 16(1), “to ensure safe and wholesome food”, stretches into deciding which foods a canteen may offer. And Article 162 adds a limit of its own: where Parliament and the State can both make laws, the State’s executive power is subject to the power a law of Parliament gives the Union. So the two routes can meet, and which one governs a canteen rule is a question this trace leaves open.

The split runs inside the Union government too. The Allocation of Business Rules give the FSS Act to the Department of Health and Family Welfare. They give “Elementary Education” and “Secondary Education” to the Department of School Education and Literacy.

So write the trace as far as it goes, and mark where it stops.

Step Answer so far
1 instrument a regulation under the FSS Act, or a State order for its own schools
2 subject the food business: the Union, under the FSS Act’s section 2; the school: Parliament and the State both (Concurrent List entry 25); public health: the State (State List entry 6); the section “Union, State or local: whose subject is it” lists every entry a canteen rule touches
3 body and provision the Food Authority, FSS Act section 92(1); or the State Government, under its executive power
4 process for a regulation: a draft for objections, the Central Government’s approval, notification, laying before Parliament (section 93); for a State order: not found in the documents held
5 who else must agree the Central Government, for a regulation
6 one sentence not yet possible: two candidate deciders
where it stopped step 3; read next the Food Authority’s list of regulations and the State school education department’s orders

The fork is the finding. The first draft, “the Health Department should ban junk food”, had hidden it behind one word.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
This trace is limited by what is held. A regulation or a State order on school canteens may already exist; this book does not hold one and does not say either way. The book in this series on India’s regulatory architecture maps the food regulators.

Matching section 2’s words to Union List entry 52 is a reading, not a ruling. Whether a canteen rule falls under the food industry, education or public health is the kind of question courts decide. The trace tells you which questions to ask. It does not answer them for you.

blocks.label: Illustration 2
blocks.html:
Now a trace that finishes. Proposal: a higher tax on sugar-sweetened drinks.

Step 1. The instrument. A rate notification. GST rates are set by notification under the GST Acts, not by a new Act each time. Find the notification now in force for the central tax: Notification No. 9/2025-Central Tax (Rate), on the e-Gazette at egazette.gov.in. Its first line names the power it uses: “sub-section (1) of section 9” of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 (the CGST Act).

Step 2. Whose subject. Article 246A(1) gives Parliament and “the Legislature of every State” power to make laws on goods and services tax “imposed by the Union or by such State”. Both.

Step 3. Body and provision. Under Article 279A(4)(e), the GST Council makes recommendations to the Union and the States on “the rates including floor rates with bands of goods and services tax”. Under section 9(1) of the CGST Act, the central tax is levied “at such rates, not exceeding twenty per cent., as may be notified by the Government on the recommendations of the Council”. So the Council recommends, and the Central Government notifies. Its notification cannot go above 20 per cent.

Step 4. Process. The Council meets and recommends. After its 56th meeting, on 3 September 2025, the Council recommended “a special de-merit rate of 40% for a select few goods and services”, as the Press Information Bureau’s release reports. The release itself says the decisions take effect through “notifications/ law amendments which alone shall have the force of law”. So the release is not the instrument. The Central Government then notified the rates. In Notification 9/2025, “the Central Government, on the recommendations of the Council, hereby notifies the rate of central tax”, and Schedule III carries 20 per cent. The first entry of Schedule III is “All goods (including aerated waters), containing added sugar or other sweetening matter or flavoured”. The notification came into force on 22 September 2025.

Notice that the release’s 40% and the notification’s 20 per cent are different numbers. The Central Government’s notification sets only the central tax. A note saying “the Union levies 40%” would be wrong.

Step 5. Who else must agree. The States. Each has a minister on the Council (Article 279A(2)(c)), and Article 246A(1) gives each State Legislature power to make laws on the GST it imposes. What each State has enacted and notified is not held for this book. Inside the Union, the Allocation of Business Rules give the GST Council and the CGST Act to the Department of Revenue in the Ministry of Finance.

Step 6. One sentence. “The GST Council recommends the rate (Constitution, Article 279A(4)(e)); the Central Government notifies the central tax under section 9(1) of the CGST Act, up to 20 per cent; the State share rests on State law under Article 246A, not traced here. The central instrument now in force is Notification No. 9/2025-Central Tax (Rate), Schedule III, as amended by Notification No. 01/2026-Central Tax (Rate), in force 1 May 2026.”

Look at who is missing from the sentence: the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. In the last section’s table it sat in the row marked “advises”.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
The trace is as current as the copies read: Notification 9/2025 and its amendment 01/2026, in force 1 May 2026, which leaves the first entry of Schedule III alone. 01/2026 names an earlier amendment, 19/2025, which this book has not read. The next Council meeting can change any of it.

The trace names who sets the rate. It says nothing about whether a higher rate would change what people drink, or about the States’ share, which sits in laws not traced here.

blocks.label: Illustration 3
blocks.html:
The third trace runs on a decision already taken, to show the whole chain from end to end. Proposal, as it might have been put before 2003: no smoking in public places. Tobacco control is the main precedent a later book in this series studies. Here it is traced only for its bodies and powers.

Step 1. The instrument. An Act, with rules for the detail. Open the Cigarettes and Other Tobacco Products (Prohibition of Advertisement and Regulation of Trade and Commerce, Production, Supply and Distribution) Act, 2003 (COTPA), on the website of the National Tobacco Control Programme, the Union health ministry’s tobacco programme (ntcp.mohfw.gov.in). Section 4 reads: “No person shall smoke in any public place”.

Step 2. Whose subject. Section 2 declares “that the Union should take under its control the tobacco industry”. It is the same form of words as the FSS Act’s section 2, and it matches Union List entry 52 in the same way.

Step 3. Body and provision. Parliament made the Act. Section 31(1) gives the detail to the Central Government: it “may, by notification in the Official Gazette, make rules”.

Step 4. Process, with its dates. The President’s assent came on 18 May 2003. An Act can be passed and not yet in force, and section 1(3) of COTPA leaves the start to dates the Central Government notifies. A notification of 25 February 2004, Statutory Order (S.O.) 238(E), appointed 1 May 2004 for sections including 4 and 31. Four years later the Central Government made the Prohibition of Smoking in Public Places Rules, 2008, “In exercise of the powers conferred by section 31”, in force on 2 October 2008. Every rule under COTPA is laid before each House of Parliament for a total of thirty days (section 31(3)).

Step 5. Who carries it out. Rule 5 makes “The authorised officers mentioned in Schedule III” competent to act on breaches of section 4. Read down Schedule III. It runs from tax inspectors to station masters, heads of hospitals, school principals and teachers, police officers, and “Representatives of Panchyati Raj Institutions”. Union, State and village officials all carry out a decision that Parliament and the Central Government took.

And the treaty. India signed the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control on 10 September 2003. It ratified the Convention on 5 February 2004. Ratifying is the step by which a country becomes a Party, bound by the treaty. Article 8(2) requires each Party to act “in areas of existing national jurisdiction as determined by national law”. Now line up the dates. The President’s assent to COTPA came nearly four months before India signed. The Act’s preamble, its opening statement of why it was made, cites World Health Assembly resolutions, the later of them from 1990, and not the Convention. The treaty binds India to act. It is not the power under which anyone in India acts. That power is section 4 and section 31.

Step 6. One sentence. “Parliament decided, in section 4 of COTPA 2003; the Central Government made the detailed rules under section 31, by notification, laid before Parliament; the authorised officers listed in Schedule III of the 2008 Rules carry it out.”

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
COTPA is read here as enacted. The Amendment Act of 2007 is not held, and the 2008 Rules are read in an unofficial consolidated print, so any later change is unchecked.

The trace shows who decided and who enforces. It shows nothing about whether smoking in public places fell, or how often the officers in Schedule III act. That is a question about carrying policy out, for the book in this series on implementation. Whether tobacco is a good template for food is a question for a later book.

points.html: The error is to name the minister who announced a measure as the body that decides it. The power to make an instrument usually sits with a body an Act names.
If you cannot fill Y with a numbered provision, you have not traced the proposal yet, and the note is not ready to send.

A press release, a speech or a meeting’s recommendation is not an instrument. The GST Council’s own release says its decisions take effect through notifications “which alone shall have the force of law”. Before you tell anyone a measure is in force, find the notification and its date.

A treaty is not the power to act. India is a Party to the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control, and the Convention itself leaves action to “national law”. When someone cites a treaty as the reason a body can act, ask for the Indian provision.
A trace that forks is a result. Write both candidate deciders, the step where the trace stopped, and the document that would settle it.
Deciding and carrying out are different jobs, often done by different people. If your proposal is about enforcement, send it to the people who enforce.

The central GST rate on sugar-added drinks is 20 per cent, in Schedule III of Notification 9/2025-Central Tax (Rate), as amended to 01/2026 (in force 1 May 2026; 19/2025 not read). The 40% in the GST Council’s release is the GST rate it recommended, not the Union’s share. Never say the Union levies 40%.
When a trainee’s proposal says “the government should”, hand it back with three blanks: X, Y and Z. Ask them to fill each from a document they can name.
Before you rely on a trace, check the newest amendment each copy names.

blocks.label: Common misreading
blocks.html: “The trace found a body with the power, so the proposal is feasible.” The trace shows that a body can act. Whether it will depends on its own priorities, on the actors pushing for and against, and on timing. None of these are in the instruments. A trace can be complete for a proposal that has no chance this year.

blocks.label: Reporting it
blocks.html: The power to make this [instrument] lies with [body] under [provision]. It would pass through [process], and needs the agreement of [other body]. Whether [body] will act is a separate question, which this note does not answer.

blocks.prompt: From memory, list the six steps of the trace in order, and write the one-sentence form the answer takes.
blocks.answer:
The six steps, in order:

  1. Name the instrument the proposal needs.
  2. Find whose subject it is: Union, State or both.
  3. Find the body that holds the power, and the provision that gives it.
  4. Find the process the instrument must pass.
  5. List who else must agree, and who carries it out.
  6. Write one sentence.

The sentence: X decides, under Y, by process Z, with W’s agreement.

blocks.prompt: A journalist has three minutes and asks: “Who can raise the tax on sugary drinks in India?” Answer without jargon, give one sentence they can quote, and say what you are not sure of.
blocks.answer:
No single body can do it alone.

The GST Council, where the Union Finance Minister and Minister of State sit with a minister from each State, recommends GST rates. The Union government then notifies its part of the tax. The States’ part rests on State law, which you have not read. The Union’s part cannot go above 20 per cent under the central GST Act.

The Health Ministry can argue for a higher tax, but it does not set the rate.

What you are not sure of: what State law says about the States’ part, and whether the latest amendments changed the entries. Say so.

Quotable sentence: “The GST Council recommends the tax on sugary drinks, and the Union government notifies its part. The Health Ministry can argue for it, but cannot set it.”

blocks.prompt:
Here is a made-up provision from a made-up Act.

“The Board may, with the previous approval of the State Government and after previous publication, by notification, make regulations to carry out the purposes of this Act.”

Name the body that makes the instrument, the instrument, the other body that must agree, and the process.
blocks.answer:
The provision, part by part:

Part In the provision
body the Board
instrument regulations
must agree the State Government, whose previous approval is needed
process previous publication of a draft, then notification

Read the provision for its verb and its subject: “The Board may … make regulations”. The words after “with” name the second decider. The words after “after” and “by” name the process.

blocks.prompt:
Here are three entries of the Seventh Schedule.

  1. Union List, entry 52: “Industries, the control of which by the Union is declared by Parliament by law to be expedient in the public interest.”
  2. State List, entry 6: “Public health and sanitation; hospitals and dispensaries.”
  3. Concurrent List, entry 18: “Adulteration of foodstuffs and other goods.”

For each, say which legislature can make laws on it, under Article 246.
blocks.answer:
Entry by entry:

Entry List Who can make laws on it
a Union List Parliament only (Article 246(1))
b State List the State Legislature, for its own State (Article 246(3))
c Concurrent List both Parliament and the State Legislatures (Article 246(2))

Entry a has a condition built into it. It covers only industries that Parliament has declared, by law, to be under the Union’s control. So before relying on it you look for the Act that makes the declaration, as the FSS Act’s section 2 does for food.

blocks.prompt:
The parts below come from a made-up trace, in no order. Write the one-sentence answer. Then say which steps the parts leave unanswered.

  • provision: section 12 of the made-up State Food Act
  • must agree: the State Government, by previous approval
  • body: the State Food Commission
  • instrument: regulations
blocks.answer:
The sentence: “The State Food Commission decides, by making regulations under section 12 of the State Food Act, with the State Government’s previous approval.”

Three are unanswered. The parts say who decides, under what and with whose agreement.

  • Step 2, whose subject: the parts never say whether the State may legislate on the matter.
  • Step 4, the process: they do not say whether a draft must be published for objections, how the regulations are notified, or whether they are laid before the State Legislature. Go back to section 12 and read the words after “after” and “by”.
  • The carry-out half of step 5: they do not say who enforces the regulations.

blocks.prompt:
Trace the proposal “Packaged foods high in sugar, salt or fat should carry a warning label” as far as these provisions take you.

  • FSS Act, section 16(1): “It shall be the duty of the Food Authority to regulate and monitor the manufacture, processing, distribution, sale and import of food so as to ensure safe and wholesome food.”
  • FSS Act, section 92(1): “The Food Authority may, with the previous approval of the Central Government and after previous publication, by notification, make regulations consistent with this Act and the rules made thereunder to carry out the provisions of this Act.”
  • FSS Act, section 93: every regulation made under the Act “shall be laid, as soon as may be after it is made, before each House of Parliament”.
  • Allocation of Business Rules, Second Schedule, Department of Health and Family Welfare, item 3(a): “The Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006”.

Then say what your trace does not settle.
blocks.answer:
The trace, step by step:

Step Answer
1 instrument a regulation under the FSS Act
2 subject the Union: the FSS Act already covers food, and its section 2 declares Union control of the food industry
3 body and provision the Food Authority, under section 92(1)
4 process a draft published for objections; the Central Government’s approval; notification; laying before each House of Parliament (section 93)
5 who else must agree the Central Government; inside it, the Department of Health and Family Welfare owns the Act

The sentence: “The Food Authority decides, by regulation under section 92(1) of the FSS Act. It needs the Central Government’s previous approval and must publish a draft for objections first. The regulation is laid before Parliament under section 93.”

What it does not settle: whether the Food Authority’s duty reaches this label at all. Section 16(1) speaks of “safe and wholesome food”, and the Act does not define “wholesome”. So whether a warning on sugar, salt or fat is within that duty is an unsettled reading, and it decides steps 2 and 3. A regulation would have to say which provision it rests on. The trace also does not settle whether such a regulation already exists, or whether the Food Authority means to act.

blocks.prompt:
A made-up district meeting proposes: “Shops near schools in the district should be stopped from selling tobacco.”

Use these facts. Section 6 of COTPA, as enacted in 2003, forbids selling cigarettes or other tobacco products to anyone under eighteen. It also forbids it “in an area within a radius of one hundred yards of any educational institution”. The National Tobacco Control Programme’s list of “Notifications on date of effect of various provisions of the Act” includes General Statutory Rules (G.S.R.) 687(E), dated 18 September 2009, “For Section- 6(b)”. Section 12(1) lets certain officers enter and search where they suspect the Act is being broken. They are police officers not below sub-inspector, and officers of a State’s food and drug regulator, authorised by the Central or State Government.

Trace the proposal. Then say what your trace does not settle.
blocks.answer:
Step 1. What instrument? Before naming a new one, check whether one exists. It does: section 6(b) of COTPA already forbids the sale within one hundred yards of an educational institution.

Step 2. Whose subject? The Union’s: COTPA’s section 2 declares Union control of the tobacco industry.

Steps 3 and 4. Body, provision and process: Parliament decided, in section 6(b), in 2003. The provision took effect through a notification about its date of effect, G.S.R. 687(E) of 18 September 2009. That notification’s own text is not given here, so the exact date it set is not known from these facts.

Step 5. Who carries it out: officers such as those section 12(1) lets the Central or State Government authorise to enter and search.

So the trace turns the proposal round. Nobody needs to decide the rule; it was decided in 2003. The district’s real request is about carrying the rule out, and it goes to the enforcing officers and to the government that authorises them. The sentence: “Parliament decided, in section 6(b) of COTPA. It took effect through G.S.R. 687(E) of 18 September 2009. Enforcement rests with officers the Central or State Government authorises, such as those in section 12(1).”

What it does not settle:

  • whether the Amendment Act of 2007 changed section 6, which is not checked here;
  • how the hundred yards are measured;
  • whether the rule is being enforced near any school in the district.

blocks.prompt:
Here are four parts of the preamble of a real instrument, the Food Safety and Standards (Packaging) Regulations, 2018, notified on 24 December 2018. The dots mark words left out.

  • “Whereas the draft of certain regulations … dated the 19th March, 2018 was published as required under Sub-section (1) of section 92 of Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 … inviting objections and suggestions from the person likely to be affected thereby, before the expiry of a period of thirty days from date on which the copies of Gazette containing the said notification was made available to the public”
  • “And whereas copies of the said Gazette were made available to the public on the 2nd April, 2018”
  • “And whereas objections and suggestions received on the said draft regulations have been considered by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India”
  • “Now, therefore, in exercise of the powers conferred by clause (k) of sub-section (2) of section 92, read with section 23 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 … the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India hereby makes the following regulations”

“Read with” means the two provisions are used together: section 92(2)(k) gives the power, and section 23 supplies the subject, the marking and labelling of foods.

You read this preamble for its dates in section 7. Now work backwards through the trace. Which steps does the preamble answer? Which does it leave out? For each one it leaves out, name the provision you would read next.
blocks.answer:
The trace, step by step:

Step What the preamble shows
1 instrument regulations
2 whose subject nothing
3 body and provision the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India, under section 92(2)(k) read with section 23
4 process a draft, objections considered, the final notification; not the approval or the laying
5 who else must agree, who carries out nothing

What the preamble does not show: part of step 4 and all of step 5. It never mentions the Central Government’s previous approval (section 92(1)) or laying before Parliament (section 93). It says nothing about whose subject this is; read section 2 of the FSS Act, which declares Union control of the food industry. It says nothing about who carries the regulations out; read section 30, under which each State Government appoints a Commissioner of Food Safety “for efficient implementation of food safety and standards”.

A notification shows its own part of the trace. The rest is in the Act, so a backward trace always ends by reading the power-giving section itself.

blocks.prompt:
Here is a worked trace. Find the steps that broke.

proposal: packaged foods high in sugar, salt or fat should carry a warning label
instrument: an order
body: the Union Minister of Health and Family Welfare
provision: the Allocation of Business Rules, which give the FSS Act to the minister’s department
process: the minister announces it
who else must agree: no one
blocks.answer:
Five lines broke, and they broke together.

The instrument is a regulation under the FSS Act, not an order. The power to make it is in section 92(1), and it belongs to the Food Authority, “with the previous approval of the Central Government”. So the body is the Food Authority, and the Central Government’s approval is a second decider.

The Allocation of Business Rules do not give anyone the power to make a food regulation. They distribute subjects among departments: they say which department deals with the FSS Act. That tells you whom to copy, not who decides.

The process is not an announcement. It is a draft published for objections, approval, notification, and laying before Parliament under section 93.

A corrected sentence: “The Food Authority decides, by regulation under section 92(1) of the FSS Act, with the Central Government’s approval, after a draft for objections.”

Why the wrong answer looks reasonable: ministers announce measures. The department really does own the Act, and the Central Government’s approval really does run through it. Each of those facts is true. None of them makes the minister the holder of the power.

blocks.prompt:
The Press Information Bureau’s release of 3 October 2024 says the Union Cabinet approved the National Mission on Edible Oils – Oilseeds. It says the Mission “will promote awareness of recommended dietary guidelines for edible oils” through a campaign. Here is a worked trace of a proposal about it. Find the steps that broke.

proposal: the oilseeds mission’s awareness campaign should tell people to use less cooking oil
instrument: an amendment to the Act behind the oilseeds mission
subject: agriculture, so the trace must find the State List entry
body: Parliament
process: a Bill passed by both Houses, then the President’s assent
blocks.answer:
The instrument line broke, and everything after it followed.

The release names no Act. It says the Union Cabinet approved a mission. That reads as an executive decision with money attached, a scheme. If an Act stood behind it, the release would be the wrong place to look, and the mission’s guidelines would say so. On the release alone, nothing needs Parliament’s vote, and no Bill is involved.

The subject line went looking for a power to make a law. No law is being made. The question for a scheme is who made it, and who can change it. The release answers the first: the Union Cabinet. How schemes are made and funded is the section on schemes and budgets.

A corrected trace: “The Union Cabinet approved the mission, using the executive power of the Union (Article 73). A change to its campaign would go to whoever runs the mission, within what the Cabinet approved.” The release does not name the department that runs the mission. The next document to read is the mission’s own guidelines, which are not held here, so the trace stops there and says so.

Why the wrong answer looks reasonable: a national mission with a long name and a large budget sounds like a law. Many people assume anything national was passed by Parliament. The release says “Cabinet”, and that one word was the place to stop.

blocks.prompt:
A made-up newspaper headline reads: “Government sets 10% cut in cooking oil.”

The words it rests on come from the Prime Minister’s radio address, Mann Ki Baat, of 23 February 2025. The Press Information Bureau released them in English: “For example, one method I suggested was ‘reducing the consumption of edible oil by ten percent (10%)’. Decide that you will use 10% less oil every month.”

Trace the headline. Then say what your trace does not establish.
blocks.answer:
Step 1. What instrument? The text is a radio address. It asks each listener to decide for themselves: “Decide that you will use 10% less oil every month.” It names no Act, rule, regulation, notification or scheme.

Steps 2 to 5 have nothing to attach to. There is no subject to place, because no law is made. There is no provision and no process, because nothing binds anyone.

The result: no body has decided anything binding. The text is a request to the public, made in a speech. The headline’s word “sets” is wrong. A correct line would be: “Prime Minister urges people to cut cooking oil by 10%.”

What the trace does not establish:

  • That no programme on oil exists. The trace read one text. A scheme or campaign could exist elsewhere, and would need its own trace.
  • That the call has no effect. A speech can put a subject on the agenda and change what people do. The trace says only that it is not an instrument.
  • Whether using less oil would change anyone’s weight. That is a question for evidence, not for a trace.

blocks.prompt:
A line from a made-up report by a public health department reads:

“We call on the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare to impose a 40% tax on sugary drinks.”

Trace the request, rewrite the line so it is addressed to the right bodies, and say what your trace does not establish.
blocks.answer:
Step 1. Instrument: a notification setting the GST rate.

Step 2. Subject: Article 246A(1) gives both Parliament and every State Legislature power over GST.

Step 3. Body and provision: the GST Council recommends rates (Article 279A(4)(e)). The Central Government notifies the central tax under section 9(1) of the CGST Act, up to 20 per cent. The State share rests on State law under Article 246A, not traced here. The Allocation of Business Rules give the GST Council and the CGST Act to the Department of Revenue, not to the Ministry of Health.

Step 4. Process: Council recommendation, then notifications. And here the trace finds something else. The Council’s 56th meeting already recommended moving sugar-added and flavoured drinks, including aerated waters, to 40%. Notification 9/2025-Central Tax (Rate) puts them in Schedule III, at a central rate of 20 per cent, from 22 September 2025. So the line asks for a rate that has already been recommended, and its central half notified.

Step 5. Who else: every State, through its minister on the Council (Article 279A(2)(c)).

A rewrite that informs rather than misdirects: “The GST Council has recommended a 40% de-merit rate for sugar-added drinks, and the central 20 per cent is in force under Notification 9/2025. Any change would be recommended by the GST Council, which moves first; the Central Government would notify the central rate. The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare can put the health case to them.”

What the trace does not establish:

  • Whether a higher rate would reduce what people drink, or obesity. That needs evidence.
  • That the Ministry of Health has no role. It is an actor that can advise and argue. It does not set the rate.
  • That the rate stands today. The trace read the notifications up to 01/2026, in force 1 May 2026, and not the amendment 19/2025 it names.
